#4800. The Psychological Origins of Fear-Based Advertising

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

When I was an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins University, I heard the story about how John B. Watson, a psychologist who is considered the father of the classical conditioning strand of American behaviorism (a term that he coined), was fired from a tenure-track position for having a sexual relationship with his 21-year-old graduate assistant, Rosalie Rayner. An earlier example of a very esteemed scholar who was fired by Hopkins for similar prurient reasons (in both cases they later married their girlfriends after becoming divorced from their first wives) involved the great philosopher, mathematician, and logician Charles Sanders Peirce. Neither man ever attained another academic post. While Watson went on to have great success outside of academia, Peirce continued as an independent scholar who lived in abject poverty, relying on financial support from many admirers, most notably his former JHU doctoral student William James, considered the father of American psychology and the co-developer, with Peirce, of the philosophical school of pragmatism.

The 1920 experiment for which Watson, assisted by Rayner, became famous (a year before they fired him, Hopkins doubled his salary in an attempt to keep him from leaving) involved an infant later known as “Little Albert.” The experiment exposed Albert, at age nine months, to various neutral stimuli–including a white rat, monkeys, and dogs–thus demonstrating his absence of fear. At age 11 months, every time that Albert reached for the white rat, a scary, loud noise (Watson striking a steel bar with a hammer behind the child’s head) occurred. The result was that the infant developed a fear response (distress and crying) to the rat even in the absence of the noise. This fear response generalized to other white objects, including cotton wool, a fur coat, and a Santa Claus mask with a white beard. Watson planned to extinguish the fear through exposure, but the experiment (today considered profoundly unethical) was prematurely ended by the child’s mother. Their scientific claim was that classical conditioning could be used to establish emotional responses, especially fear, in children.

In 1928, Watson and Rayner (who went on to have two children together) co-authored a child-rearing book, “Psychological Care of Infant and Child” in which they used the results of their experiment to argue (based on zero evidence) that a child’s personality is formed entirely by environmental forces with no role for innate nature or instincts. The book’s most controversial–and, to me, horrifying–advice for parents was that they should not hug, kiss, or show affection to their children, in order to toughen them up for the grim world they would face as adults. Interestingly, Watson and Rayner had two sons, both raised according to their no-love method. As adults, both attempted suicide, one of them successfully. (A third adult child, a daughter from Watson’s first marriage, also attempted suicide, and blamed it, whether fairly or not, on her father).

After being forced out of academia, Watson was hired by the New York-based advertising company J. Walter Thompson. He thrived there, eventually becoming a vice-president of the firm. The basis of Watson’s success as an ad man was developing the idea, based on his view of behaviorism, that the key to persuading consumers to buy a particular product was conditioning them to the idea that by not buying it they were exposing themselves or their loved ones to a feared physical or social danger. In the physical realm, Watson persuaded consumers to buy Scott’s toilet paper by showing doctors grimly surrounding a patient whose medical condition was attributed to wiping their bum with “harsh toilet tissue.” Another ad campaign, on behalf of the Johnson & Johnson company, emphasized to mothers that they were exposing their children to dread diseases by not purchasing the company’s hygiene products. But fear was also used as the basis for Watson’s ads in the social domain, with one example involving buying a brand of toothpaste not to promote good dental health but to avoid the social rejection that supposedly flows from bad breath and discolored teeth.

Watson thus pioneered in America the use of psychological concepts as the basis for advertising campaigns, grounding it on the conditioning of emotional responses, particularly fear. He was followed in the related field of public relations by Edward Bernays, a double nephew of Sigmund Freud (his mother was Freud’s sister and his father was the brother of Freud’s wife), and who based his ideas of propaganda–the title of his most famous book–not on behaviorism but, very loosely, on psychoanalytic theory. Bernays, whose parents moved from Austria to the US when he was an infant, often visited his uncle (who gifted him Cuban cigars, perhaps in thanks for getting one of his books published in America) and was a pioneer in the field of public relations. Although not himself trained as a psychoanalyst, Bernays claimed to have developed a public relations theory based on his famous uncle’s notion that people’s actions are controlled less by conscious ideas than by unconscious desires and fears.

Bernays, like Watson, was successful in promoting commercial products, with his biggest success, influenced by advice from Freud’s translator A.A. Brill, occurring on behalf of the American Tobacco Company. The purpose of that campaign was to persuade women to overcome the taboo against female smoking by portraying Lucky Strike cigarettes as phallic symbols empowering women to escape from male oppression. Bernays’ efforts, however, were mainly in the public sector, and involved such activities as drumming up support for America’s entry into WWI. Years later, when working for the United Fruit Company, Bernays promoted the CIA-led overthrow of the left-leaning President of Guatemala, Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán. In that campaign, Bernays took a page from the John B. Watson playbook by portraying Arbenz as a communist who posed a threat to the U.S. and its people. Bernays later followed the same Red-Scare playbook in the early days of the Vietnam War, but later backed off from the effort when that war became unwinnable, both in the field and in the realm of public opinion.

Bernays justified his efforts at propaganda (a term he stopped using when it began to take on negative connotations) by claiming that it was essential in a democracy for its leaders to have a way to keep the populace from spiraling out of control. Although Watson did not address the role of advertising in a democracy, he shared with Bernays the idea that people’s actions are governed mainly by emotion, and that psychology provided emotion-based mechanisms of social control. Neither Watson nor Bernays showed any concern about the need to base their arguments on actual truth. Ominous implications for the future of democracy in the U.S. and other countries flow from the ubiquity of political advertising based on fear-mongering that in many cases is based on completely made-up facts. It is in the political arena, more than in his dangerous advice to parents, that the lessons from John B. Watson’s Little Albert experiment have come to have profound influence on public life.

#4798. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Bezzy communities provide meaningful connections with others living with chronic conditions. Join Bezzy on the web or mobile app.

Can't get enough? Connect with us for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4797. Job Crafting at 25

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Twenty-five years ago, Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton published a paper that asked readers to look at work a little bit differently. Rather than viewing jobs as something organizations designed and employees simply carried out, they argued that employees could reshape their work in ways that make it more meaningful, engaging, and sustainable. They called the process job crafting.

I recently spent several days sifting through two special issues of the Journal of Business and Psychology, 41(3) and 41(4), marking the 25th anniversary. Together, they contain 19 papers. Individually, each paper tackles a fairly specific question. Collectively, though, they tell a much bigger story. I've whittled that bigger story down to three takeaways that really stood out to me.

The first thing that struck me was how much the questions have evolved over 25 years.

The original paper introduced job crafting as a new way of thinking about work. Unsurprisingly, much of the early research focused on understanding whether job crafting was associated with outcomes like engagement, well-being, performance, and job satisfaction. That was an important first step. Researchers first needed to establish what job crafting was, how it could be measured, and whether it was linked to meaningful workplace outcomes.

Reading these special issues, though, it became clear that the conversation has moved forward. Very few papers were still asking whether job crafting was generally associated with positive outcomes (we’ve established that), and the ones that did were mostly examining the issue through the lens of contextual factors. Instead, researchers were asking much more specific questions about how the process actually unfolds.

For example, Parker et al. (2026) examined whether the relationship between work characteristics and job crafting is reciprocal rather than one-directional, arguing that employees shape their jobs while their jobs simultaneously shape their opportunities to craft. Another, Rudolph et al. (2026), explored whether the effects of autonomy and workload follow nonlinear patterns, suggesting that too little or too much of either may actually reduce employees' ability to craft their work.

Other papers asked equally nuanced questions. Does job crafting operate differently for younger and older employees (Schepp & Boehm, 2026)? What role does job crafting play for interns transitioning into the workforce (Kim et al., 2026)? How might employees with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder use job crafting to better align their work with their strengths and challenges (Weinhardt et al., 2026)?

The broader message from all these papers is that there doesn't appear to be a single formula for effective job crafting. What works depends on the person, the job, and the situation. That may not sound particularly exciting, but I actually see it as a sign that this research domain has matured. Once researchers become reasonably confident that an idea is important, they start asking more interesting questions about how people can make it work. After 25 years, job crafting research seems to have reached that point.

The second thing that struck me was how much the idea itself has expanded.

The original paper described three broad ways employees could craft their work: by changing the tasks they performed, the relationships they developed, and the way they thought about their jobs. Twenty-five years later, researchers are applying that same basic idea in a variety of new directions.

These special issues included papers on career crafting, which extends the concept beyond one's current job to the broader arc of a person's career (Li et al., 2026); team job crafting, which examines how groups of employees collectively reshape their work (Wang et al., 2026); and time-spatial job crafting, which explores how employees intentionally structure where and when they work in hybrid environments (Demerouti, 2026). The introductory article also positioned playful work design in the same context as job crafting, another bottom-up approach to proactively shaping work (Bakker & Slemp, 2026).

None of those ideas felt like a stretch to me. In fact, they all seem to build naturally on the original insight that employees aren't simply passive recipients of the jobs organizations create. Instead, they can actively shape their own work experiences.

What I found most interesting wasn't any single extension. It was realizing how pliable the original idea has proven to be. Twenty-five years later, researchers are still finding new ways to apply the basic insight that employees don't simply have to adapt to work—they can actively shape it. More importantly, that insight is no longer confined to an individual employee crafting an individual job.

The third thing that stood out to me was how much more nuanced the conversation has become. Early job crafting research often focused on demonstrating that employees who crafted their jobs tended to experience better outcomes. The anniversary papers paint a more complicated picture. They increasingly ask when job crafting helps, when it doesn't, and what factors influence whether it succeeds.

For example, Rudolph and colleagues argued that more job crafting isn't necessarily better. Like many workplace behaviors, there may be a point where additional crafting provides diminishing returns or even becomes counterproductive. Additionally, Parker and colleagues suggested that the relationship between job crafting and positive work outcomes may not simply run in one direction. Rather than job crafting causing engagement or well-being, employees who are already engaged or thriving may also be more likely to craft their jobs, creating an ongoing cycle of mutual influence.

Other papers highlight the importance of context. Schepp and Boehm explored how job crafting changes across the lifespan, suggesting that what works for a younger employee may not be the same as what works later in a career. Weinhardt and colleagues examined how ADHD shapes job crafting, reminding us that individual differences matter as well.

To me, this is perhaps the most important evolution. Rather than treating job crafting as a universally beneficial phenomenon, these papers recognize that its effects depend on the circumstances. That's ultimately a much more useful way to think about job crafting because it shifts the focus from encouraging more crafting to understanding what kind of crafting is likely to help, for whom, and under what conditions.

Reading through these special issues turned out to be far more interesting than I expected. Many of the papers were less about introducing new ideas than about taking stock of how job crafting has evolved over the past 25 years. That evolution resulted in researchers asking better questions, applying the concept in new contexts, and developing a more nuanced understanding of when job crafting actually helps.

If there's a practical lesson from all of this, it's that work is probably more flexible than we often assume—but not infinitely so. Most of us have at least some ability to shape how we experience our jobs. The trick, though, isn't simply to craft more. It's to understand which changes are actually likely to make work better for you in your particular role and circumstances.

#4795. sonnen files for insolvency in Germany as US sales double

Residential battery storage maker sonnen is reporting two very different stories today: Its German business has filed for insolvency, while sonnen USA says sales have doubled and it’s preparing to expand.

The insolvency filing comes just two months after Shell sold sonnen to investment group TIVEN. Germany’s Handelsblatt reported that sonnen GmbH confirmed the filing and informed roughly 400 employees in Wildpoldsried, Bavaria, on October 22.

For homeowners with sonnen batteries, the immediate question is what happens to service. According to Handelsblatt, the company intends to keep supporting its more than 150,000 existing customers. But a substantial overhaul is coming: Numerous subsidiaries are expected to be wound down or enter insolvency proceedings under self-administration, with only one production site remaining. The report does not identify that site.

Meanwhile, sonnen USA’s announcement describes a growing home battery business. The company says sales have doubled and production has tripled year over year, supported by expanded manufacturing in Stone Mountain, Georgia. It expects to deliver more than 180 megawatt-hours of residential battery storage in 2026.

Much of that growth comes from virtual power plants (VPPs). These connect home batteries so they can work together to support the grid, giving households another way to earn value from their solar and storage systems.

In Texas, sonnen says its SOLRITE offering serves more than 6,000 homes, combining rooftop solar, batteries, energy management, and VPP participation. In Massachusetts, its sonnenCommunity program offers cash rewards to participating homeowners in National Grid and Eversource territories. The company also reports rising sales through its Wattsmart program in Utah.

TIVEN bought the entire global business, including sonnen USA. US CEO Blake Richetta stated today that “TIVEN is firmly committed to the long-term success of sonnen USA as a strong, market-leading company in the North American VPP energy market.”

TIVEN stated that it “looks forward to bolstering the company’s impressive growth.”

But the US announcement leaves an important question unanswered: How will the German restructuring affect the US operation and its customers? It doesn’t address the insolvency filing, and sonnen USA declined to comment on developments in Germany when contacted by pv magazine.

The US growth figures show demand for sonnen’s batteries. What customers still need is a clear explanation of how manufacturing, software support, and service will be maintained through the restructuring.

#4794. Another megawatt-level charger enters China: 300 miles in 5 minutes

Chery has announced a 1.44 megawatt charging system, able to deliver 500km (311 miles) in 5 minutes. And it’s not even the fastest system available in China.

It’s become common knowledge at this point that Chinese EVs are the world’s state of the art, but the country isn’t sitting on its laurels, it’s still racing to compete with newer and better technology.

A case in point has been the country’s DC fast chargers, where we’ve seen a slew of announcements of new systems in just the last year.

BYD has a 1.5MW charger which it has already installed 10,000 of, Geely just announced a 2.2MW charger, and CATL has a hyper-fast charging battery.

The competition is so fierce that firms are starting to compete over seconds, not minutes of charging time.

And now, a new challenger appears: Chery.

Chery announced a 1.44MW charger that can add 500km (311miles) of range to a battery in 5 minutes, and can charge from 10-97% in 6 minutes and 50 seconds, as reported by CarNewsChina.

The numbers put it in league with the best of the best in the country. Per CarNewsChina’s accounting, the new Chery “Volt-Dragon” battery is the second-fastest at reaching 97% state of charge, 23 seconds behind CATL’s 6 minute, 27 second record time. FAW, Geely and BYD are all between 8 and 9 minutes for the same full charge metric.

Some other firms released times for charging in very cold or very warm weather, which Chery declined to release during its announcement. Though it did say that it could still deliver 500km of range in 8 minutes in “conservative scenarios.”

Could it be the drugged out Elon Musk is more into politics and taking over the world than advancing EV technology at an electric car company.

In Chery’s announcement, it dropped the same buzzword as Geely did: “AI-Powered.” Chery calls its system CheryMind, and supposedly it adjusts charging power based on temperature changes within the battery, to help maintain optimal charging speeds and battery health.

Meanwhile in the US, the fastest public chargers are around 400kW, with 750kW potentially coming next year. That’s all plenty quick enough for refueling, especially on a roadtrip, but for high-throughput DC charging locations, especially those in urban areas where some people might not have a consistent parking spot to charge in (and yes, we need to fix that), higher speed chargers can relieve a lot of pressure.

Chery has only just started installing chargers, and says it will have 100 chargers open in 10 Chinese cities soon. It plans to install 20,000 stations worldwide by 2029, which is quite a bit slower than BYD’s target to have 20,000 chargers installed by the end of this year.

#4793. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Bezzy communities provide meaningful connections with others living with chronic conditions. Join Bezzy on the web or mobile app.

Can't get enough? Connect with us for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4792. What if a Chatbot Really Could Be a Friend?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Co-authored by Ryan Moore, Ph.D., assistant professor, iSchool and School of Computing, the University of Texas at Austin.

My daughter bought me a label maker for my birthday. I had never considered using a label maker. But suddenly, the leftovers in the freezer required a name and a date, the file drawers in my office needed topic indicators, and the boxes with holiday decorations are now clearly marked with what is inside. Who knew that something you never had could be so indispensable?

Chatbots may be the label makers of the social world. We never knew how useful they could be until they arrived. A chatbot, especially when powered by today’s generative artificial intelligence (AI) models, can feel like talking with another person. With names like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, chatbots may play important and unique roles in our social lives.

New technologies present exciting opportunities, but also reasons to be cautious or concerned. These new AI tools usher in concerns about job obsolescence, security, and the environment. But when used appropriately, AI tools could enhance our social lives in meaningful ways. Let’s focus on enhancement here, not substitution.

I’ve mentioned previously that different types of social ties fulfill diverse social needs: belongingness, information, everyday tasks, support, intimacy, and feeling loved and cared for. No single social tie fulfills all needs. We benefit from a mix of romantic partners, children, friends, neighbors, close acquaintances (i.e., fringeships), and even strangers.

Historically, new technologies introduced possibilities for social interaction. For example, since the first part of the 20th century, when the telephone entered everyday life, we commonly talk with people who aren’t present.

Chatbots differ from technologies that facilitate communication between people. Chatbots can perform autonomous social functions when humans aren’t available. They provide individualized, tailored information; a sounding board to strengthen human relationships; a forum to think aloud without managing another human’s reactions; and they can reinforce decisions. Consistent affirmation has several limitations and could harm more than help us, but if the input is weighed for what it is, it can be supportive.

Why wouldn’t we want to add that to our social repertoire?

In the 1980s, L.L. Bean advertised a 24-hour retail service that you could call toll-free day or night. This was a novel approach, but it was limited to ordering fishing gear or a jacket.

Chatbots are available to discuss anything, anytime, anywhere. You can wake them at 2 a.m. when you are ruminating about a talk you have to give. And they have no expectations of reciprocity. There are hotlines available anytime, too (if you ever feel suicidal, call 988 to speak with a human—not a chatbot). But chatbots will shoot the breeze.

Other available software keeps a calendar. A chatbot goes a step further by solving problems, generating a schedule, and tailoring an agenda to your needs and priorities. Chatbots determine the information we need, then find it.

Chatbots may also support people with deficits. They can take notes during a class for a student with a learning disability. Someone in early-stage dementia can ask the chatbot the same question repeatedly, without taxing a caregiver.

Chatbots can help with tasks that require detail or repetition. It can tutor a third grader in multiplication tables over and over and never needs to go fix dinner. It can format or update a spreadsheet and quickly pull information from the web. Human effort may be better spent on the complex steps in each project.

Counterintuitively, Chatbots could enhance our human relationships. Communication between people can benefit from input that balances what you want with predictions of another person’s reactions. Chatbots offer:

In 2000, a search engine called Google spread widely, accessing a universe of information. The website even became a verb. I googled, “the year Google became popular” to land on 2000.

But chatbots can personalize information. With the prompt: “I want a vacation that balances sites, hiking, and great food,” ChatGPT suggested Tucson, Arizona. Over time, the chatbot remembers my preferences.

It has pulled recipes (simple, pescatarian), recommended books, and culled my movie recommendations. No one crafts your personal time the way your chatbot can in minutes.

Any particular relationship comes with constraints. You don’t hug your customers. You don’t send memos to your grandma. Chatbots are additions to our social networks, but limitations make them tools rather than social partners.

Chatbot advice can be harmful on important issues, including finance or health. Issues of consequence require human research and input; chatbots have led people severely astray.

Researchers have identified addictive or compulsive engagement, overreliance for cognitive skills, and psychological and emotional dependence on chatbots. Some people have even formed romantic ties to a chatbot. Collectively, these behaviors pose risks for individuals who most need human contact.

Their constant affirmation can be limiting. Chatbots won’t engage in detrimental aggression. But human disagreements provide fodder for complex thinking and problem-solving. Challenges of communicating with people who disagree have been linked to prolonged life. AI chatbots affirm human actions even in cases where those actions are deceptive or illegal, which could cause users to take actions that harm their real-world relationships.

Finally, although nearly all our technology use consumes electricity, the AI powering today’s chatbots poses environmental impacts that we should be mindful of.

Bottom line: Chatbots serve as a beneficial “extra” in a diverse social network. But as with any technology, you must implement it effectively. Dishwashers are great for everyday plates and cups, but don't use them for the cast iron skillet.

Using a chatbot wisely can enhance your social world in new and exciting ways. But stick to what it does best.

Boyd, R. L., & Markowitz, D. M. (2026). Artificial intelligence and the psychology of human connection. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 21(2), 192–220. https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916251404394

Dagnino, F. M., Fante, C., Guerrieri, V., & Passarelli, M. (2026). Addicted, attached, or just delegating? A scoping review on “problematic artificial intelligence use”. Frontiers in Psychology, 17, Article 1900953. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900953

Folk, D., Yu, S., & Dunn, E. (2024). Can chatbots ever provide more social connection than humans? Collabra: Psychology, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.117083

#4789. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Bezzy communities provide meaningful connections with others living with chronic conditions. Join Bezzy on the web or mobile app.

Can't get enough? Connect with us for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4788. Overhead wired charging comes to Austin electric bus fleet

CapMetro’s Austin transit fleets electrified two public bus lines and opened two new park-and-ride facilities featuring overhead pantograph-style wired charging equipment to help Austinites breathe a little bit easier.

Originally announced in June, CapMetro’s two new park-and-ride stations are now open. Dubbed the Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center facilities debuted alongside the agency’s Rapid 800 and 837 electric bus routes, adding upgraded passenger amenities and end-of-line charging infrastructure to support its growing fleet of electric transit buses.

At CapMetro’s main bus depot, infrastructure partner Camber Charging supplied and installed two 1,440 kW charging systems connected to 48 industrial dispensers. The installation provides 2.9 MW of total charging capacity, and is designed to support overnight charging for up to 48 electric buses simultaneously.

The new Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center terminals extend that infrastructure along the Rapid 800 and 837 routes with the overhead pantograph chargers that are the big news here, allowing buses to top off their batteries at the end of each line and eliminate any lingering range anxiety for the trip back.

“Instead of a typical bus holding 8 hours of charging, on-route charging takes that out to 20 to 22 hours,” explains CapMetro Chief Operations Officer and Executive VP, Andy Skabowski. “Every time that pantograph drops, we charge that bus. That’s what makes a commitment like (every) 10- to 15-minute service possible.”

The buses themselves are built on Canadian manufacturer New Flyer’s Xcelsior battery-electric transit platform (battery specs aren’t included in the release, but New Flyer claims up to 660 kWh of available capacity). And, with up to 320 all-electric hp with all its torque available at 0 rpm, the city’s 48 electric buses will have no problem navigating Austin’s stop-and-go traffic.

This seems like a logical cost effective solution. In theory, this should enable transit systems to purchase busses with smaller batteries which would surely offset the cost of the new charging infrastructure.

Camber Charging provides preventive maintenance, charger and energy management software and remote diagnostics across all three locations.

SOURCE | IMAGES: CapMetro, via Charged EVs.

#4787. An Abandoned Pacifier Stirs a Moving Conversation

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

My friend told me about an experience that jolted her the other morning. She is my age, give or take a few years, and the mother of two adult daughters.

She was walking near the Hudson River when she spotted an upturned pacifier/dummy on the ground.

This image brought a flood of memories for her and became a visceral reminder of her own early mothering days. She told me about this, and I immediately connected with her experience. We gave ourselves the space to indulge our own imaginings and immerse ourselves in our individual inner worlds.

There is something embedded in the form of a dummy, which is intriguing. Maybe it's the shape, adapted from the maternal breast, and the meaning this can hold. Maybe it's something about the maternal collective unconscious and our need to soothe our child at any cost; our hope of harmony with our infant. The pacifier is also a gauge of social judgement; do "good mothers" use them?

My friend’s story took me back to the early days of my mothering. For me, the dummy played a prominent part in the mothering of each of my children. It represented an almost sacred object holding the potential of a peaceful retreat for my infant and myself.

A similar playbook emerged for each of my children. Each time, there was an initial resistance to the dummy, quickly followed by acceptance as my baby ceded to its comfort.

I remember the wonder of watching my baby’s rhythmic sucking, the fluttering of the eyes. Then, a momentary halt to the sucking, as if he forgot. Then, the sucking started again. I was mesmerized watching my baby remembering and forgetting, her eyes fluttering while drifting off to blissful sleep in her own world; being aware of the dummy one minute, and then unaware.

This was often followed by a release of the dummy, a realization, and a cry as it was gently returned to his mouth so the sucking could continue. This became a regular routine which brought confidence and solace. A respite for both of us.

Then, my memories shifted to that of my older infant’s cot filled with dummies one minute, then empty the next. My infant never tired of this game of throwing and retrieving it.

It has dawned on me that this game held so much meaning for my later understanding of mothering. The importance of laughter and games and the reality that the dummy, like the mother, is both necessary and dispensable over time.

Then, my thoughts began to meander back to this particular dummy left on the street. What is its story?

Is there a baby crying and screaming for it? How will the baby and the mother manage without it?

Who lost it? Maybe the father? The grandmother? Did a sibling throw it out? Was it older children or teenagers playing with it for a stunt?

Was this an infant’s planned farewell to this dummy?

Is there a mum somewhere ferreting through her diaper bag to find it, or is she looking for another, saying to herself, “Why did I only bring one?”

The anticipated and real screams from her baby, and worrying about how she would soothe her.

What about characteristics of the dummy itself? Is it pink or blue or maybe white? Is it new or old? What does this tell us about the baby?

Is it a newborn’s dummy? Is it one of those new ergonomic ones, which is a reminder of the years that have passed since my own hands-on mothering and what has changed?

Then, some truths about dummies/pacifiers:

For some women, a dummy has no meaning, and for others it means so much.

The idea of a dummy is also wrapped up in the social and inner discourse of judgment. In my day, there was a lot of narrative surrounding the use of dummies, many shoulds and should nots. Does a good mom give her baby a dummy? Is she lazy? Will it damage her baby’s bite and teeth? If you give your child one, how do you get rid of it? Will he still be walking around with it at 3 or 4 years of age?

Questions such as these return to the everlasting judgment and moral reckoning that mothers continually endure and can hopefully challenge.

My friend’s story of the dummy abandoned on the ground provokes reflection:

For the current hands-on mother, the dummy captures multiple moments, thoughts, and possibilities of her everyday life: The many challenges that are embodied in the face of an inconsolable child. The mother’s constant striving to soothe her child, to do her best, and the reality that there is a continual struggle between her own and her baby’s needs and questions about how these are balanced.

It is a reminder of the social judgment that surrounds the mother, where she really needs compassion, support, and encouragement to name and manage her daily life and her feelings. Our job as post-hands-on mothers is to champion this cause.

For mothers such as myself and my friend, while we are no longer hands-on, we own our memories. They are treasures that we forever hold that belong only to us and one day to our daughters. Moments of bliss, connection, and struggle are embodied in the image of a dummy.

The power of these objects offers a valuable and seamless conduit back to that time and into the future, embodying what we are as mothers, immortalizing our maternal memories, and continuing to enrich our lives.

#4786. Yozma IN 11 review: The OG mini e-moto gets updates galore

…including 4.5kW motor, bigger 1.4kWh battery and 45mph top speed

Yozma may not have invented the mini moto space, but they certainly helped mainstream it. Together with Tuttios and Sur Rons, Yozma’s IN10 was one of the most popular mini motos out there, and if you surveyed the average group of 14-15-year-olds in a suburban rideout, you’d be hard-pressed not to find at least a few Yozma IN10s among them…

Today Yozma is shipping the IN 11 ($100 off with code 9TO5TOYS100), which attempts to bridge the gap between entry-level mini-bikes and high-end off-roaders, but at what cost?

Taken in a vacuum, the Yozma IN11 is an impressive update to the IN 10 and actually is more closely specced to the bigger IN10 Pro.

But we of course, don’t live in a vacuum, and others, including the Heybike Villain and the Engwe Eagle have already brought 52V, 4.5kW motors to the pit bike form factor, sometimes at much lower cost.

I should say here that parents who want to keep their kids’ e-motos in the 20-30mph range are going to be a whole lot happier with the 2.6kW than 4.5kW motors. Two nice safety improvements over the original Yozma IN10 include the magnetic kill switch and brake lights on the IN11.

If we are keeping it real here, there are dozens of similar-sized and spec’d mini-e-motos out there, often at a much lower cost than the Yozma IN11. But I’d argue that as the biggest and most trusted of these brands, Yozma is a safer bet.

Also, the IN11 is just a lot more solid than the random Amazon/Alibaba electric pit bike. Putting the IN11 together is quicker and easier than any other emoto I’ve built, and it just feels a lot more solid.

That feeling extends to the safety features. The brakes are more dialed in. The turning feels a lot tighter, and the overall ride is quieter and lighter. I believe, and my limited testing bears this out, that spec for spec, I got a lot more range on the IN11 than I got on other bikes with similar battery and motor specs. That 200nm of torque feels like it belongs on a much more expensive e-moto.

The smart wheelie mode is a nice trick (15, 25, or 40 degrees wheelie settings) and something we’ve only seen on Anylands for this price point so far. It is less of a standout feature on the IN11, and we expect to see this on just about every new pit bike coming out over the next few years. In fact, we’ve got another one in the review queue now.

That said, the price, which is currently fluctuating between $1299 and $1499 (don’t forget your $100 off 9TO5TOYS100 code), Yozma is going to be on the more expensive side of the 4.5kW emotos out there and some of the less established and more sketchy newcomers are bringing an intense value competition to the place where Yozma once dominated by itself.

#4783. Is Weight Loss Less Valid Without Struggle?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

We tend to admire people who achieve difficult things through determination, sweat, and effort. Someone who spends years dieting, resisting cravings, and losing weight is often praised for their discipline. But what happens when another person achieves a similar result with the aid of medication? Does the achievement become less meaningful because it required less effort?

I find this question particularly interesting in the context of GLP-1 medications. Much of the discussion around semaglutide and tirzepatide has focused on their effectiveness, safety, and cost. These are important considerations, but they do not fully explain why people can have such different reactions to its use. Some regard medication as a sensible way to improve their health. Others are uncomfortable with the idea of relying on it, even when they recognise its potential benefits.

It would be easy to attribute these differences to concerns about side effects or distrust of pharmaceutical interventions. Both matter, as research on attitudes toward anti-obesity medication suggests (Le Roux et al., 2025). Yet I think there is another psychological question worth examining: How much of our sense of achievement depends on believing that we accomplished something through our own effort?

Consider what self-control typically means in everyday life. We associate it with resisting temptation, suppressing desires, and making difficult choices. Someone who wants a slice of cake but decides against it is exercising restraint. We admire that restraint because we recognise the internal conflict involved.

GLP-1 medications complicate this understanding. Research involving semaglutide suggests that treatment can influence food cravings and certain eating-related experiences (Wharton et al., 2023). If someone experiences fewer cravings, the psychological demands of managing their eating may also change. They might not need to resist temptation to the same extent because the temptation itself has become less prominent.

I think of this as motivational quieting. By this, I mean a reduction in how frequently or intensely a desire captures someone's attention. It is a conceptual distinction rather than an established clinical measure, but one that may help us understand the psychological experience of appetite regulation.

What interests me is the difference between successfully resisting a desire and no longer experiencing that desire as strongly in the first place. Both can contribute to behavioural change, but they involve different experiences of effort.

And this is where questions about identity become relevant. If someone has spent years believing that successful weight management requires discipline and sacrifice, medication may challenge that belief. They may welcome the relief while simultaneously questioning how much credit they can take for the outcome. This reaction is not necessarily irrational. People attach meaning to the processes through which they achieve their goals, not merely to the results. However, problems arise when effort becomes a moral standard against which we judge other people's health decisions.

Research on obesity stigma has repeatedly shown how beliefs about personal responsibility influence attitudes towards weight (Ringel & Ditto, 2019; Westbury et al., 2023). Beames et al. (2016) also examined how perceived effort shapes evaluations of weight loss. These findings raise an uncomfortable question: Why are we sometimes more impressed by the suffering involved in achieving a result than by the result itself?

The emergence of GLP-1 medications makes this question difficult to ignore. People who use pharmaceutical assistance can be judged differently from those who achieve weight loss through diet and exercise (Sprengholz et al., 2026). Such judgements may reveal less about the person taking medication than about our cultural expectations surrounding discipline and deservingness.

Choosing not to use a GLP-1 medication does not automatically indicate a concern about identity or self-control. People have legitimate reasons for declining treatment, including side effects, medical circumstances, affordability and personal preferences. These considerations should not be reduced to psychological resistance, nor should anyone feel morally obliged to accept medication.

Still, I suspect that our reactions to GLP-1 medications tell us something important about the way we define personal agency. We often assume that having control means being able to resist what we want. But perhaps control can also involve choosing circumstances or interventions that make certain desires easier to manage.

This leaves me with a question that extends well beyond weight management: If two people reach the same goal, but one experiences considerably less struggle along the way, why are we so quick to treat the harder journey as the more admirable one?

Beames, J. R., Black, M. J., & Vartanian, L. R. (2016). Prejudice toward individuals with obesity: Evidence for a pro-effort bias. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 22(2), 184–195. https://doi.org/10.1037/xap0000079

Le Roux, C. W., Koroleva, A., Larsen, S., & Foot, E. (2025). Anti-obesity treatment preferences of healthcare providers and people living with obesity: A survey-based study. Clinical Obesity, 15(1), e12704. doi.org/10.1111/cob.12704

Post, S. M., Stock, M. L., & Persky, S. (2025). Comparing the impact of GLP-1 agonists vs. lifestyle interventions and weight controllability information on stigma and weight-related cognitions. International Journal of Behavioral Medicine, 32(4), 528–540. doi.org/10.1007/s12529-025-10353-2

Ringel, M. M., & Ditto, P. H. (2019). The moralization of obesity. Social Science & Medicine, 237, 112399. doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2019.112399

Sprengholz, P., & Klöckner, M. (2026). Stereotypes and discrimination toward weight loss injection users. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 56(7), 528–537. doi.org/10.1111/jasp.70070

Westbury, S., Oyebode, O., van Rens, T., & Barber, T. M. (2023). Obesity stigma: Causes, consequences, and potential solutions. Current Obesity Reports, 12, 10–23. doi.org/10.1007/s13679-023-00495-3

Wharton, S., Batterham, R. L., Bhatta, M., Buscemi, S., Christensen, L. N., Frias, J. P., Jódar, E., Kandler, K., Rigas, G., Wadden, T. A., & Garvey, W. T. (2023). Two-year effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg on control of eating in adults with overweight/obesity: STEP 5. Obesity, 31(3), 703–715. doi.org/10.1002/oby.23673

#4782. Why volunteers are gluing seeds to clam shells in Connecticut

Published Oct 24, 2026 11:18 AM EDT

Environmental restoration sometimes requires out-of-the-box thinking. Along the waters of Long Island Sound in New York and Connecticut, experts are tackling the challenge of restoring crucial eelgrass habitats by gluing the plant’s seeds to clams.

Eelgrass (Zostera marina) is an important member of the ecosystem. It provides foraging areas and shelter for young fish and invertebrates, diminishes coastal erosion, draws in excess nutrients, filters water, and releases oxygen, for instance. Compared to the 1930s, eelgrass meadows in and around Long Island Sound have decreased by more than 90 percent, according to regional environmental action group Save the Sound.

To make matters worse, eelgrass is difficult to restore and there have been a lot of failed attempts, Bill Lucey, a Long Island Soundkeeper from the organization, tells Popular Science. In 2025, the team tried a different approach—recruiting clams as underwater gardeners. The strategy was originally ideated by Robert Vasiluth, the founder of Submerged Aquatic Vegetation EngineersEnvironmental (SAVE) .

The approach consists of attaching eelgrass seeds to the clam’s shells. When the clams are released into the sound, they bury into the sediment, taking the seeds down to the bottom and effectively planting them. When they conducted drone imagery to check in on their results this year, they found that the eelgrass meadow coverage had increased by 178 percent.

“It needs to survive for three years before we can really trumpet our horns and say it’s working, but the actual method of putting clams out and seeds attached to them really worked. The generation of the plants was incredible,” Lucey explains.

During their 2025 planting, the team used glue typically used in coral reef restoration to attach seeds to the clams. But then Connecticut College biologist Maria Rosa yielded better germination rates when she used wet pieces of rice paper (the kind you make spring rolls with) to seal the seeds against the shell. The Save the Sound team asked its volunteers to do the same earlier this week.

“The problem with the spring roll wrappers is yesterday [Monday, October 19], when we deployed them for the first time in scale, they weren’t all staying on,” says Lucey. “So what we’ve started doing today [Tuesday, October 20] is putting a little pocket of seeds, 10 to 20 eelgrass seeds on the top of the clam, putting a little circle of this [coral] glue around it, and then putting the spring roll wrapper stamp over that and wetting it. And so it keeps the seeds moist, and the glue holds the spring roll wrapper to the clam till it dissolves, and then it’ll release the seeds next to the clam.”

Save the Sound is aiming to release 10,000 claims and 300,000 seeds this season.

Correction: The original article misspelled Maria Rosa’s name. It has since been updated.

#4780. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Bezzy communities provide meaningful connections with others living with chronic conditions. Join Bezzy on the web or mobile app.

Can't get enough? Connect with us for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.

#4779. 6 ways bats are surprisingly human

Published Oct 24, 2026 1:30 PM EDT

Bat Week officially begins today. It’s the one week where Earth’s only winged mammals get top billing. Often associated with disease, vampires, and other generally unpleasant things, bats are actually important pollinators and play critical roles in our ecosystem.

“They’re just so cool and so interesting. During first forays into bat studies, it was just one question after another,” Rachel Page, an evolutionary biologist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama, tells Popular Science. “The more I sort of scratched the surface, the more interesting it became—which is the fun part.”

One reason bats are so interesting to scientists like Page is that they are surprisingly similar to humans. Here’s how.

Sharing a meal with good company brings immense joy for us humans. For many vampire bat species (subfamily Desmodontinae), sharing food is a matter of survival. They survive exclusively on blood and can only go about two nights without a blood meal before they die. To get around this, they rely on their social networks.

“They have the equivalent of friends. Basically, if a bat comes back from a night of foraging and has not been successful, other members of that social group will share food,” Page explains. “They’ll regurgitate blood for the bat that came back hungry.”

If that donor bat has difficulty getting food later, the one recipient will often become the donor. “So there’s this very reciprocal relationship,” says Page.

According to Page, bats will have their distinctive personalities just like people. It’s present across species, but also individual bats as well.

“You have some species that are very feisty, and they’ll go out of their way to pick a fight, and then other ones that are much more passive, calm, and very gentle,” she says.

At the edge of Panama’s Soberanía National Park, tiny, fruit-eating bats will take over the roost of larger, carnivorous bats. The Seba’s short-tailed bat (Carollia perspicillata) weighs roughly the same as a strawberry. By comparison, the frog-eating, fringed-lipped bat (Trachops cirrhosus) weighs roughly as much as an apricot and twice as much as the short-tailed bat.

Page and her colleagues in Panama have witnessed fights between the two species from roosts set up throughout the forest.

“Basically, it was the male Seba’s short-tailed bat who was instigating the fight. He was coming over and was kind of boxing and threatening much larger bats with wide open mouths and lots of teeth,” Page recalls. “And he just kept at it, and then finally, this group of fringed-lipped bats left.”

Even in the thick jungles of Panama, bats can find motionless insects on leaves. Initially, scientists believed that the thick tree cover would give small insects an “acoustic camouflage” that would confuse a bat’s echolocation system. But they were wrong.

The bats can see through this acoustic camouflage by changing the angle at which they approach the still insect.

“If you approach a flat leaf at just the right angle, you can actually get an echolocation signature,” Page explains. “You can get an echolocation signal that jumps back at you, but only if you direct your echolocation call at just the right angle.”

That’s exactly what the bats were doing in order to find insects who tried to hide in leaves.

When it’s time for the babies to wean or leave the roost, mother tent-making bats (Uroderma bilobatum) will physically prod their young with their forearms.

“There is this interesting tug that you see across so many different species. For birds, when they’re ready to fledge, there’s this sort of uncertainty.”

When sick, humans and even non-human primates change their behavior. We isolate so that the disease does not spread, and will look to plants and other sources of medicine for relief. Bats appear to change their diet to less nutritious leaves. While this may sound backwards, it’s in the hope that they have medicinal properties.

In an ongoing study with a team from the Ukrainian Bat Rehabilitation Center, the Smithsonian team is looking at the bats from Barro Colorado Island in Panama.

“We have fecal samples from these bats, so we were able to see exactly what they are eating,” says Page.

In addition to changing their diets, vampire bats will self-isolate when they are sick and others will act in a way familiar to any human parent—continuing to care for our young, even when sick.

“You don’t do as many of the normal behaviors unless it’s taking care of your babies,” says Page. “And again, it’s like a human relationship. If your little kid has a fever, you’re not going to shut them in a room and leave them. You’re not going to desert them.”

To find dinner, the fringe-lipped bat (Trachops cirrhosus) will listen in on their prey’s mating calls. These frog-eating bats eavesdrop on the mating calls that the male frogs use to attract females. They then use the calls to assess if the frog is edible or poisonous before going in for the kill.

“They’ve really cracked this communication of another entire group,” says Page.

According to Page, it’s similar to being in a quiet room and hearing someone open up a bag of potato chips and is loudly eating. The noise makes everyone pay attention. “Bats attend to those acoustic signals of other bats, and that attention then helps them learn,” Page says. “They can learn those distinctions of palatable versus poisonous, and they can learn that socially as well from observing the other behaviors with bats.”

To learn more about bats and how to help protect them, visit Bat Week’s website.
